name: Omar Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a line contractor, not the power company itself, so we get hired out wherever there's work, new subdivisions, rebuilds, and storm response. When a big storm hits somewhere, we load up and drive, sometimes twelve hours, and work double shifts restoring power for a week or two. I love storm work, the towns come out and wave at the trucks. What wears me out is never knowing where I'll be sleeping next Tuesday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with the time you're not on the road?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fly drones, mostly. I've got a commercial drone licence and I do some photography for estate agents on weekends, extra cash. I use AI for basically everything, planning routes, learning the drone software, even meal plans, which my mates find hilarious. I'm single, I rent a small flat I'm hardly ever in, and I've got maybe three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected too much. I'd probably post that the tools are good for little stuff and leave the big predictions to the guys selling them. Not a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, nothing much. My job's mostly hands and trucks. I'd just keep using the tools for what they're good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working storm season, keep the drone side gig going. Maybe use AI to help me figure out the best time to buy a used bucket truck, I've thought about starting my own small outfit one day. Keep saving at the same pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now, which is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for almost everything. What would stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Route planning, studying, writing quotes for the drone jobs. It's like a mate who's read every manual. It doesn't have to change the world to be worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep doing the drone work on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, definitely. It's fun and it pays for my holidays. Might even grow it a bit.

S0.say: I'd say it's still useful and people just expected too much. The tools are good for small things, and the big predictions belong to the people selling them.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, because my job is mostly hands and trucks. I'd just keep using the tools for what they're good at.
S0.do: Keeps working storm season with the contractor and keeps the weekend drone photography going. Uses AI for planning and quotes, keeps saving at the same pace and mulls buying a used bucket truck someday.
S0.feel: Calm; same as now, which suits him.
S0.quote: It's like a mate who's read every manual.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is an easygoing heavy user of AI with a drone side business and an itch to run his own outfit someday. He sees no threat in the plateau. His relationship with the tools is practical, not starry-eyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who move early. If you're willing to learn, there's going to be new work. I'd probably say that more than once, which might annoy people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Drone inspections, robot-assisted line work, the companies will need people who know the trade and the tech. That's literally me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get certified on whatever new inspection drones and line robots the contractors are buying, as soon as courses come out. I'd pitch my boss on a drone inspection service, me running it. And I'd grow my weekend drone business into inspections for small solar farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. This one feels like my lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned drone inspections. Is that already happening on your jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bits of it. Some utilities already use drones to check lines after storms, before they send crews. I've flown a couple for our foreman on the side. If that becomes standard, I want to be the guy who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the other guys on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would be fine, some would hate it. Dmitri, he's fifty, he'd rather quit than look at a screen. I'd try to help him, but you can't make someone learn.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people who move early, because there will be new work if you're willing to learn. I'd probably say it more than once.
S1.think: Privately I think it's good for me. Companies will need people who know both the trade and the tech, and that's exactly me.
S1.do: Gets certified on new inspection drones and line robots as soon as courses appear. Pitches his boss on a drone inspection service he'd run, and grows his weekend drone work into solar farm inspections.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited; this feels like his lane.
S1.quote: If that becomes standard, I want to be the guy who runs it.
S1.fieldNote: Omar sees steady disruption as an opening, not a threat, because his hobby lines up with where the job is heading. He's already flown drones for his foreman unofficially. He's sympathetic to Dmitri but pragmatic that you can't force someone to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be rough for everyone, and governments need to put a floor under people. I'm not usually the one asking for help, but this is different. I'd say it straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose the main job pretty quick. Contractors are first to go when budgets get tight, and if robots can do storm work, nobody needs to drive us twelve hours. My edge with the tech helps, but in two years everyone's edge disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the drone and robot side. Try to get hired to supervise or maintain the robots, or set up as a small subcontractor that deploys them. I'd cut my spending and push savings toward six months, and I'd be willing to move anywhere the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel like I could do something, but it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drone side gig might not save you here. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if AI can do anything, it can fly drones and sort photos too. My weekend thing is great now, but in that world it's worth nothing. I'd have to be selling something it can't do, maybe just being the human who's responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday I'd been planning to Portugal. Then eating out. My rent's not huge, so I'd keep the flat, but I'd look at sharing it.

S2.say: I'd say this will be rough for everyone and governments need to put a floor under people. I'm not usually one to ask for help, but this is different.
S2.think: I think I'd lose the main job fast, since contractors go first when budgets tighten. My tech edge helps, but in two years everyone's edge disappears.
S2.do: Goes all in on supervising or maintaining robots, or deploying them as a small subcontractor. Cuts spending, starting with a planned trip to Portugal, pushes savings toward six months and is ready to move anywhere for work.
S2.feel: Anxious, still able to act, but it's tight.
S2.quote: My weekend thing is great now, but in that world it's worth nothing.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario wipes out Omar's two advantages, early tech skills and the drone business, and he sees that clearly. Contractor status makes him feel more exposed than utility staff. He stays action-minded and is the most willing so far to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years, okay, time to move. People should start learning now. That's what I'd say at work and probably post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in decent shape if I start right away. Five years is enough to build a small drone and robot inspection business and get known before the big companies roll in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the drone business properly in the first few months, buy a better inspection drone, maybe ten thousand, partly from savings. I'd take courses on the robot systems, and keep doing line work while I build it. If the business got going, I'd go part-time with the contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big storm job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be chasing anything. With five I can actually build something that's mine and have time to make mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want your own outfit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but different. Not a bucket truck, a robot fleet. Maybe three or four robots and a van. That would be wild.

S3.say: I'd say five years means it's time to move and people should start learning now. That's what I'd say at work and probably post.
S3.think: I think I'd be in decent shape if I start right away. Five years is enough to build a small drone and robot inspection business before the big companies arrive.
S3.do: Registers the drone business in the first few months and spends about ten thousand, partly from savings, on a better inspection drone. Takes courses on robot systems and keeps line work going until the business can carry him.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like before a big storm job.
S3.quote: Not a bucket truck, a robot fleet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Omar from defensive to entrepreneurial: he'd invest savings in equipment and build a business. His dream of his own outfit survives but changes shape. He's willing to take real money risk on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people just need to start thinking about it now. There'll be new work, there always is. I'd be pretty upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do fine, even well. Ten years to build skills and a business is a lot. The main risk is me getting lazy because it feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working line jobs for a few years while building the drone business. I'd take proper training in robotics, maybe a diploma part-time. By year five I'd want to be running inspections full-time, and by the time AGI arrives I'd want to own some of the machines, not just work for whoever does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a buzz, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At thirty-seven, what would your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running my own thing, a handful of robots, a couple of people, contracts with the utility for inspections and storm work. Maybe a partner, maybe a house. Not on the road all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies just buy everything and squeeze out small guys like me. That happens in every industry. So I'd need to be good and quick, and have the contracts locked in early.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people start thinking about it now. There'll be new work, there always is, and I'd be pretty upbeat about it.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd do fine, even well, with ten years to build skills and a business. The main risk is getting lazy because it feels far off.
S4.do: Keeps doing line work for a few years while growing the drone business and studying robotics part-time. Aims to run inspections full-time by year five and to own some machines by the time AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a bit of a buzz.
S4.quote: By the time AGI arrives I'd want to own some of the machines, not just work for whoever does.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Omar sounds genuinely hopeful and talks about owning machines rather than competing with them. His one honest worry is that big companies squeeze out small operators. He named his own laziness as a risk, which I didn't expect.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out my edge. What would help is some kind of income floor for a year or two, and the utilities giving small local businesses a fair shot at robot work instead of just signing with giant firms. And cheap training, fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about storm work. When the lights go out in a town, people come out and bring you coffee. I'd miss that. A robot fleet won't get the coffee.

headlineQuote: When the lights go out in a town, people come out and bring you coffee.
portrait: Omar Quinn is a 27-year-old lineworker for a contractor, driving across regions for storm response and rebuilds, who flies drones and does weekend photography for estate agents. He's single, rents a flat he's hardly ever in, has about three months saved and uses AI for nearly everything. Pragmatic rather than political, he sees steady change as a chance to build his own drone and robot inspection business. He turns anxious only when two-year AGI wipes out his head start, and with more warning he plans to own machines rather than compete with them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it wipes out his edge with technology and his drone side business.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor for a year or two, fair access for small local firms to utility robot contracts, and cheap, fast training.
